Categorical variables: why not analyse means; what is analysed instead; contingency table structure
column2:
• numbers attached to categories arbitrary → "mean" meaningless, depends on category sizes
• analyse frequencies: counts per combination of categories
• contingency table ($r \times c$): cell counts, row totals, column totals, grand total $n$

column1: Pearson's chi-square ($\chi^2$) test of independence: purpose; null hypothesis ($H_0$); core idea
column2:
• tests association between two categorical variables
• $H_0$: variables independent (no association)
• compare observed ($O$) vs. expected ($E$) frequencies under independence
• large deviation → association

column1: Chi-square ($\chi^2$) test of independence: formulas for expected frequency, test statistic, degrees of freedom (df)
column2:
• $E_{ij} = \frac{\text{row total}_i \times \text{column total}_j}{n}$
• $\chi^2 = \sum_{ij} \frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}}$, over all cells; dividing by $E$ standardises
• $df = (r-1)(c-1)$; $2 \times 2$ table → $df = 1$

column1: Chi-square ($\chi^2$) test: decision rule; critical values at $\alpha = 0.05$ for degrees of freedom (df) 1, 2, 3
column2:
• reject $H_0$ if $\chi^2$ > critical value
• df = 1: 3.84
• df = 2: 5.99
• df = 3: 7.82

column1: Chi-square ($\chi^2$) test of independence: assumptions; remedy if violated
column2:
• independence: each participant/entity contributes to only one cell
• expected frequencies > 5; larger tables: ≤ 20 % of cells ≤ 5, none ≤ 1
• violated → Fisher's exact test
• no normal or continuous data required

column1: Fisher's exact test: motivation compared with chi-square ($\chi^2$) test; typical use; limitation
column2:
• $\chi^2$ test relies on approximate $\chi^2$ distribution → unreliable for small samples / low expected counts
• Fisher (1922): computes exact probability
• small samples, usually $2 \times 2$ tables
• larger tables possible but computationally heavy; large samples → $\chi^2$ sufficient

column1: Fisher's exact test: probability of a $2 \times 2$ table (cells $a, b$ / $c, d$; fixed margins); p-value
column2:
• $P = \frac{(a+b)!\,(c+d)!\,(a+c)!\,(b+d)!}{a!\,b!\,c!\,d!\,n!}$
• equivalent: $P(a) = \binom{a+b}{a}\binom{c+d}{c} / \binom{n}{a+c}$
• p-value = sum of probabilities of observed table + all more extreme tables

column1: Lady tasting tea experiment (Fisher): design; result; p-value; conclusion
column2:
• 8 cups: 4 tea-first, 4 milk-first; must pick the 4 tea-first cups
• 3 of 4 correct; $H_0$: random guessing
• $P(T=3) = \binom{4}{3}\binom{4}{1}/\binom{8}{4} = 16/70$; $P(T=4) = 1/70$
• $p = P(T \ge 3) = 17/70 \approx 0.243$ → fail to reject $H_0$
• one-tailed: only better-than-chance performance counts

column1: Non-parametric tests: definition; typical basis; when useful
column2:
• assumption-free / distribution-free (no normality, equal variances, …)
• often based on ranks (high values → high ranks)
• skewed data, ordinal data, small $n$

column1: Non-parametric tests compared with parametric tests: advantages; disadvantages
column2:
• advantages: fewer assumptions; handle ordinal / non-normal data; robust to outliers
• disadvantages: usually less powerful if parametric assumptions hold; less informative about magnitude of differences

column1: Wilcoxon signed-rank, Mann–Whitney U, Kruskal–Wallis tests: data design; parametric counterpart
column2:
• Wilcoxon signed-rank: 2 paired samples ↔ paired t-test
• Mann–Whitney U (= Wilcoxon rank-sum): 2 independent groups ↔ independent t-test
• Kruskal–Wallis: > 2 independent groups ↔ one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA)

column1: Wilcoxon signed-rank test: hypotheses; assumptions
column2:
• $H_0$: median difference = 0
• $H_1$: median difference ≠ 0
• paired observations
• differences symmetric around the median

column1: Wilcoxon signed-rank test: procedure; decision rule
column2:
• difference $d$ per pair; drop zero differences
• rank $|d|$; ties → average rank
• reattach signs; sum positive ($W^+$) and negative ($W^-$) ranks
• $W = \min(W^+, W^-)$
• reject $H_0$ if $W \le W_{crit}$ (smaller $W$ = stronger evidence)

column1: Mann–Whitney U and Kruskal–Wallis tests: null hypothesis ($H_0$); procedure
column2:
• Mann–Whitney $H_0$: both groups from same distribution (no median difference)
• Mann–Whitney: pool & rank all observations → rank sums per group → $U$ → compare with null distribution
• Kruskal–Wallis $H_0$: all groups same median
• Kruskal–Wallis: rank all together → rank sums per group → $H$ → compare with $\chi^2$ distribution

column1: Statistical test assumptions: why check them (doorbell analogy); examples
column2:
• broken assumptions → misleading conclusions
• doorbell: assume bell works, no answer → "friend dislikes me"; bell was broken
• examples: normality, independence, equal variances, expected counts > 5

column1: Permutation test: purpose; key assumption; sampling scheme; when useful
column2:
• tests group difference in any statistic (mean, median, proportion, …) without distributional assumption
• group labels exchangeable under $H_0$ (same distribution); normality not needed
• sampling without replacement from pooled data: each observation once per permutation, group membership changes
• small samples, non-normal data, unusual test statistics

column1: Permutation test: steps; p-value; exact vs. approximate version
column2:
• observed statistic → pool observations → shuffle labels, recompute statistic
• repeat (1,000–10,000×) → permutation distribution under $H_0$
• p-value = proportion of permuted statistics as or more extreme than observed; reject if $p < \alpha$
• very small samples: enumerate all permutations (exact); larger: random permutations (approximation)

column1: Bootstrap: purpose; sampling scheme; uses
column2:
• estimate sampling distribution of a statistic
• resample with replacement; same size as original sample
• standard errors (SE), confidence intervals (CI), also hypothesis testing
• when analytical formulas hard to derive; parametric & non-parametric contexts

column1: Bootstrap: steps; standard error (SE) formula; 95 % percentile confidence interval (CI); inference from CI
column2:
• resample (each group) with replacement, ≥ 1,000×
• compute statistic each time (e.g. mean difference, regression coefficient, correlation)
• $SE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{B-1}\sum_b (t^*_b - \bar{t}^*)^2}$, $B$ = number of resamples
• 95 % CI $= [t^*_{2.5\%},\ t^*_{97.5\%}]$
• CI excludes 0 → significant difference; sign → direction

column1: Permutation test vs. bootstrap: sampling; what is resampled; what the distribution represents; main output; key assumption
column2:
• sampling: permutation without vs. bootstrap with replacement
• resampled: group labels of pooled data vs. observations from the sample
• distribution: statistic under $H_0$ vs. sampling variability of the statistic
• output: p-value vs. SE / CI
• assumption: exchangeability under $H_0$ vs. sample represents population
